title: Rex, the little dinosaur
summary: Rex is the smallest in his family, but he has a huge roar that scares even the clouds.

scenes.text:
A very, very long time ago, before there were cars or cities, in a green valley full of giant ferns and volcanoes puffing smoke, lived a dinosaur named Rex. But not just any Rex. Rex was the smallest dinosaur in his whole family, and that made him a little sad.

His parents were so enormous that the ground shook under their footsteps.

They could step on a whole tree without noticing. His brothers and sisters were huge too, and their tails looked like tree trunks. Even his great-aunt, who could barely walk anymore, was huge: her neck was so long it reached the clouds.

But Rex was small, shorter than a sunflower, lighter than a big rock, with shiny green scales and two short horns on his head. Sometimes he felt invisible, as if the others stepped on him without meaning to. But Rex kept a secret: the only giant thing he had was his roar.

When he roared with all his strength, GRROOOAAAR!, the highest leaves of the trees trembled, the insects ran away, and waves rose in the puddles. But Rex almost never roared, because he was afraid of his own voice.

One sunny morning, while Rex was skipping flat stones across a clear stream, he heard a cry. It was a sharp, frightened cry. Rex lifted his head and swiveled his ears like two antennas, paf, paf.

The cry was coming from some nearby bushes. Rex walked over there slowly, intrigued. And he saw something that broke his heart: an orange butterfly, with wings as bright as the setting sun, had been trapped under a giant branch.

The branch was enormous, heavy, gray, much bigger than Rex. The butterfly flapped her wings desperately, unable to escape, and her eyes were full of tears. "Help, help!"

she squeaked in a thin voice. Rex looked around: his parents were far away, eating on the other side of the valley. His brothers and sisters too.

He was alone. For a second he wanted to run off and find someone bigger. But the butterfly looked into his eyes, and Rex knew what he had to do.

Before roaring, he closed his eyes and breathed.

Then he filled his lungs until his belly puffed up like a balloon, opened his mouth, and roared with all his might: GRRRROOOAAAAAR!

The roar was so, so loud that the ground shook as if there were an earthquake. The leaves came loose from the trees and flew through the air, forming a green cloud. The birds shot out of their nests, the lizards ducked under the rocks, and even the distant volcanoes seemed to sigh.

And the giant branch, the one that seemed impossible to move, jumped into the air as if it were a feather. It landed far away, on a soft bush, without hurting anyone, and the whole valley heard the thump.

The butterfly was free at last, she flapped her wings and went flying.

She did pirouettes in the sky, went up, came down, drew a figure-eight in the air, and then came over to Rex and landed on his nose. She gave him a soft kiss. "You are small, but very, very powerful," she told him in a sweet voice.

"Thank you, thank you, thank you so much." Rex turned red with pride and didn't know what to say, so he smiled with all his teeth. The butterfly circled him twice more and left happily toward the sun.

That afternoon, while the sun was setting and painting the sky in oranges and pinks, Rex walked back to his nest slowly, thinking, thinking. On the way he passed a stream.

He saw his reflection in the water and stood looking at himself for a while. He looked the same as always: small, green, with his two horns. But inside, something had changed.

His roar had always scared him. He had always thought it was an ugly, noisy, frightening thing. Even he himself was sometimes scared of his own voice.

But today he had discovered something new, something important. His roar wasn't for scaring others. His roar was for helping.

It was a special tool that nature had given him, precisely because he was the smallest and needed a big power. When he reached the nest, his mom welcomed him with an enormous kiss on his forehead. Rex curled up against her warm, scaly belly and there, happy, he fell asleep.

That night he dreamed of all the small creatures he would be able to help the next day: ants, butterflies, beetles, birds. And his roar never scared him again.
